scenario: Quarterly security pass: about 400 route handler files each need the identical audit step for missing authorization checks, every finding must be adversarially verified before it is reported, and next quarter the whole pass should rerun the same way from a single command.
primary: Dynamic workflow: a script fans out one auditor subagent per file, a verifier stage cross-checks findings, and the run is saved to .claude/workflows/ as a reusable slash command
rejected_alternative: Spawning many parallel subagents directly from the main conversation
rejection_reason: The main agent coordinates subagents turn by turn and every result returns to its context window; at 400 items that exceeds what one conversation can coordinate (20 concurrent subagents and 200 per session by default), and the orchestration is not repeatable. The workflow runtime runs dozens to hundreds of agents per run (up to 1,000, 16 concurrent), keeps intermediate results in script variables instead of any context window, and a saved run reruns as /<name>. This is the docs' own 'audit many files for the same issue' shape.
context_boundary: isolated context (each spawned agent has its own context; intermediate results live in script variables, and only the final report reaches the session)
lifecycle: explicit invocation: 'use a workflow' or the ultracode keyword in a typed prompt, later the saved /<name> command; a launch approval prompt gates the run per permission mode
failure_mode: Stopping mid fan-out is expensive on resume: cached results stop at the first unfinished agent and every agent started after it reruns; exiting Claude Code forfeits resume entirely (resume works only within the same session); no mid-run user input is possible.
version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later; paid plans only; on Pro it must be enabled from the Dynamic workflows row in /config

scenario: A production service drops the connection after exactly one message and nobody knows why. I want five investigators working in parallel, each owning a different hypothesis, actively trying to disprove each other's theories like a scientific debate, with whatever consensus survives written to a findings doc.
primary: Agent team: a lead session spawns five teammates who share a task list and message each other directly through their mailboxes
rejected_alternative: Five parallel subagents launched from the main conversation
rejection_reason: Subagents only report results back to the agent that spawned them and never talk to each other, so the adversarial cross-examination cannot happen; each investigator would anchor on its own theory with no one challenging it. Teammates are full independent sessions with direct inter-agent messaging, and the competing-hypotheses debate is the documented flagship team use case: the theory that survives active disproof attempts is more likely the real root cause.
context_boundary: independent sessions (each teammate is a full Claude Code session with its own context window)
lifecycle: explicit spawn request in the prompt, or Claude proposes teammates and the user confirms; requires the experimental env flag set at session start
failure_mode: Task status can lag when a teammate fails to mark work complete, blocking dependents; the lead may declare the team finished early or start doing the work itself; in-process teammates do not survive /resume; token cost scales linearly with teammate count.
version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default; requires CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in settings.json or the environment

scenario: Running our test suite prints tens of thousands of lines. I want the suite run and only the failing tests with their error messages reported back, and the raw output must never enter the conversation I am working in.
primary: One subagent: delegate the test run so the verbose output stays in the subagent's own context and only the failure summary returns
rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow
rejection_reason: This is a single self-contained side task where only the result matters, the exact case the subagent docs name under 'isolate high-volume operations'. A workflow adds a launch approval prompt, a background runtime, and generated script scaffolding to run what is effectively one agent; the workflow docs reserve the mechanism for jobs that outgrow a handful of subagents or need the plan held in code. Scale machinery buys nothing here.
context_boundary: isolated context (subagent transcript is a separate file and window; only the final report returns to the caller)
lifecycle: model-decided delegation matched from the task description, or guaranteed for one task with an @-mention
failure_mode: The returned report still lands in the main context, so a poorly instructed subagent can return a huge result and defeat the isolation; background subagents (the default) also run with a reduced built-in tool set.
version_caveat: none (subagents run in the background by default as of v2.1.198)

scenario: One feature cuts across the frontend, the backend API, and the test suite. I want three workers, each owning one layer, keeping each other informed as the interface contract evolves during the work, and I want to drop into any individual worker directly to redirect it without going through an intermediary.
primary: Agent team: one teammate per layer, coordinating over direct messages and a shared task list, with each teammate a full session the user can open and message from the agent panel
rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow with one stage per layer
rejection_reason: A workflow accepts no mid-run user input and its agents never converse; the plan is frozen in the script, so an interface change discovered by the backend agent cannot be negotiated with the frontend agent. Cross-layer coordination (frontend, backend, tests each owned by a different teammate) is one of the four documented strongest team use cases, and direct user-to-teammate interaction is exactly what teams add over every other mechanism.
lifecycle: explicit spawn request naming the three roles; requires the experimental env flag at session start
failure_mode: Two teammates editing the same file overwrite each other, since teams do not isolate teammates in worktrees; the work must be partitioned so each teammate owns different files, and coordination overhead plus token cost grow with team size.
version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default; requires CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1

scenario: Run the strict type check, fix whatever it reports, run it again, and keep looping until it passes or two consecutive rounds make no progress. Nobody should babysit the loop or re-decide anything between rounds.
primary: Dynamic workflow: the script holds the check-fix-recheck loop and the deterministic two-rounds-no-progress termination condition
rejected_alternative: Chaining subagents turn by turn from the main conversation
rejection_reason: With chained subagents the model re-decides after every round and each round's results land in the main context, so a long loop both drifts (the stop condition is judgment, not code) and bloats context. The workflow docs give this exact prompt as a canonical shape ('keep fixing until a check passes... or two rounds in a row make no progress'): the script owns the iteration and the stop condition, and the session receives only the final outcome.
context_boundary: isolated context (per-round agents; loop state and round results held in script variables)
lifecycle: explicit invocation via the workflow request or ultracode keyword, or a saved command; approval prompt at launch
failure_mode: No mid-run user input, so if a fix genuinely needs a human call the run cannot pause to ask; a loop that stalls without triggering the stop condition burns agents toward the 1,000-agent per-run cap; exiting the session loses resumability.
version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later; paid plans; Pro enables via /config

scenario: Migrate roughly 500 component files from one styling library to another. Every file gets the same transform, each performed in an isolated copy so edits never collide, and each result is verified before it counts as done.
primary: Dynamic workflow: discover the file list, fan out one transform agent per file working in an isolated copy, and run a verify step per result
rejected_alternative: An agent team splitting the migration among teammates
rejection_reason: Teams scale to a handful of long-running peers coordinated by a lead's turn-by-turn judgment, and teammates are not isolated in worktrees, so avoiding edit collisions means manually partitioning 500 files. A large identical-step migration is the workflow's documented home turf: dozens to hundreds of agents per run, per-item isolated copies, and a scripted verification stage; the docs give this exact 'migrate many files in parallel' prompt.
context_boundary: isolated context (per-file agents in isolated copies; results collected in script variables)
lifecycle: explicit invocation with the per-run approval prompt; savable as a command for later migration waves
failure_mode: Interrupting mid fan-out reruns every agent that started after the first unfinished one, even completed ones; the Large workflow warning (over 25 agents or 1.5M projected tokens) is advisory only and does not pause the run, so cost needs active watching.
version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later; paid plans; Pro enables via /config

scenario: A 60-file pull request needs a correctness review of every changed file, one reviewer per file, then all per-file findings merged, deduplicated, and ranked into a single summary. The reviewers have nothing to discuss with each other; only the merged output matters.
primary: Dynamic workflow: fan out one reviewer agent per changed file, then hand all findings to a single merge agent that ranks and deduplicates
rejected_alternative: An agent team of reviewers
rejection_reason: Parallel code review is a documented team use case, which makes this a genuine near-miss, but the team version splits review by lens (security, performance, coverage) across a few peers who share and challenge each other's findings. Here reviewers are per-file, the docs' team comparison says to choose based on whether workers need to communicate (these do not), 60 workers exceeds the 3-to-5 teammate guidance, and the merge is a deterministic collect-and-reduce step; the docs list this exact 'review every changed file and write one summary' workflow shape.
context_boundary: isolated context (per-file reviewer agents; findings flow through script variables to the merge agent)
lifecycle: explicit invocation; naturally saved as a command to rerun on every branch
failure_mode: The single merge agent gates the whole deliverable, so weak deduplication or ranking buries valid per-file findings; a stopped run reruns all agents that started after the first unfinished one on resume.
version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later; paid plans; Pro enables via /config

scenario: Three specialists must run in strict sequence: one finds performance issues, one fixes exactly what was found, one verifies the fixes. Each step consumes the previous step's output, and all three work in the same handful of hot files.
primary: Chain subagents in sequence within one session: the main agent runs each specialist and passes the relevant results to the next
rejected_alternative: An agent team with three specialist teammates
rejection_reason: The three-specialists framing suggests peers, but the steps are strictly dependent and touch the same files. The team docs say exactly that: for sequential tasks, same-file edits, or work with many dependencies, a single session or subagents are more effective, and concurrent teammates editing the same files overwrite each other. The subagent docs document this chaining pattern directly ('use the code-reviewer subagent to find issues, then the optimizer subagent to fix them'), giving each specialist isolation while the caller carries forward only the needed context.
context_boundary: isolated context (each subagent starts fresh; the main agent relays results between steps)
lifecycle: model-decided delegation, steered by naming the subagents in the prompt
failure_mode: Handoff loss: the main agent summarizes between steps, so detail the next specialist needed can be dropped; each returned result also accumulates in the main context across the chain.

scenario: Before committing to a design for a new developer tool, I want it explored from three angles at once, user experience, technical architecture, and a devil's advocate, with the perspectives reacting to each other's arguments as they form, and I want to jump into any one explorer mid-flight and redirect it.
primary: Agent team: three teammates with distinct perspectives who message each other directly, each a full session the user can open and steer while it works
rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow that drafts the design from several independent angles and weighs them
rejection_reason: Workflows explicitly support drafting a plan from several angles and weighing them against each other, which makes this the near-miss, but workflow agents never converse and the run accepts no mid-run user input, so neither the live cross-perspective argument nor the mid-flight redirection is possible. This three-perspective exploration with a devil's advocate is the team docs' own first-team example, and direct teammate interaction is the capability teams uniquely add.
lifecycle: explicit spawn request describing the three roles; requires the experimental env flag at session start
failure_mode: An unattended team drifts and wastes effort (docs: monitor and steer, letting a team run too long unattended increases wasted work); the lead may synthesize before teammates finish and must sometimes be told to wait.
version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default; requires CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1

scenario: A review pass over recent changes should dispatch an independent verifier for each finding it produces, typically 5 to 10 findings, and none of the per-finding verification chatter should ever reach my conversation. I want exactly one final verified summary back.
primary: One subagent that spawns nested subagents: the reviewer delegates a verifier per finding and only the top-level summary returns to the session
rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow with a review stage and a verify stage
rejection_reason: The fan-out is real but small and hangs entirely off one delegated task. The subagent docs name this exact shape as what nesting is for: 'a reviewer subagent that dispatches a verifier per finding, so the intermediate output never reaches your main conversation', with subagents able to spawn up to three layers below the main conversation by default. At 5 to 10 agents the workflow's launch approval, background runtime, and generated script buy nothing; workflows are for jobs that outgrow a handful of subagents.
context_boundary: isolated context (a nested subagent tree; intermediate results are confined to it and only the top-level summary returns)
lifecycle: model-decided delegation; nesting occurs inside the reviewer subagent when its tool list includes Agent and depth allows
failure_mode: At the depth limit the Agent tool is withheld and the leaf agent does the verification itself; verifier detail is only as visible as the reviewer's synthesis, so a weak summary hides verified evidence; every spawn counts against the 200-per-session subagent cap.
version_caveat: Nesting depth defaults to three layers as of v2.1.219, configurable via CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH (v2.1.217+); v2.1.217 to v2.1.218 defaulted to one layer, and v2.1.172 to v2.1.216 allowed five

scenario: New teammates and every fresh session re-learn the same basics: the monorepo builds with pnpm build:all, tests need a local Postgres, and API handlers live under src/api/handlers/. The team wants Claude to hold these facts in every session, shared with everyone through version control.
primary: Project CLAUDE.md at ./CLAUDE.md (or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md), committed to the repo
rejected_alternative: A project skill whose description covers build and layout questions
rejection_reason: A skill's body loads only when invoked or judged relevant, so these facts would be absent from most sessions. The docs direct always-needed facts (build commands, conventions, project layout) to CLAUDE.md and reserve skills for procedures and on-demand reference material.
lifecycle: Loaded in full at session start for every session launched in or below the project directory
failure_mode: Adherence degrades as the file grows (docs advise targeting under 200 lines), and the content is advisory context, so Claude can still deviate from it

scenario: Generating release notes here is a 30-step procedure with a fixed template, a changelog query script, and formatting conventions. It runs about once a week, and the write-up is far too long to keep pasting into chat.
primary: A skill: .claude/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md with the template and script as supporting files
rejected_alternative: Adding the procedure to the project CLAUDE.md
rejection_reason: CLAUDE.md loads in full at every session start, so a rarely used 30-step procedure would tax context and adherence in every session. The docs say a CLAUDE.md section that has grown into a procedure rather than a fact should move to a skill, whose body costs nothing until it is used. This is the always-on-fact versus sometimes-procedure boundary.
lifecycle: The description sits in the skill listing every session; the full body loads when the user types /release-notes or Claude matches the description to the request
failure_mode: Weak description keywords mean Claude never auto-invokes it and users forget the command exists, so the procedure quietly stops being followed

scenario: There is a scripted workflow that drops and reseeds the shared staging database. The team wants the steps encoded once and runnable on demand with a single short command, but the assistant must never decide on its own that a reseed is warranted, no matter how relevant the conversation looks.
primary: A skill with disable-model-invocation: true in its frontmatter, run only when the user types /reseed-staging
rejected_alternative: A normal skill whose description says 'only run when the user explicitly asks'
rejection_reason: By default Claude can invoke any skill whose description matches, and a warning inside the description is only advisory text. disable-model-invocation: true removes the skill from Claude's listing and blocks Skill-tool invocation entirely; the docs recommend it precisely for side-effect workflows like /deploy where the user must control timing.
lifecycle: Loads only when the user types the slash command; the description is not placed in Claude's context otherwise
failure_mode: The flag gates skill invocation, not the underlying commands: if the model reconstructs the same destructive steps outside the skill, nothing blocks them (that requires a PreToolUse hook or permission deny rules)
version_caveat: none for the core flag; from v2.1.196 it also blocks the skill from running when a scheduled task fires with it as the prompt

scenario: The API package has strict conventions (every endpoint validates input, uses the standard error envelope, carries OpenAPI comments) that only matter when someone touches src/api/. The root instructions file is already near its useful size limit and adherence is slipping.
primary: A path-scoped rules file: .claude/rules/api.md with paths frontmatter such as ["src/api/**/*.ts"]
rejected_alternative: Appending the conventions to the project CLAUDE.md
rejection_reason: CLAUDE.md loads unconditionally every session and the docs advise keeping it under about 200 lines because longer files reduce adherence. Path-scoped rules load only when Claude works with files matching the globs, so the conventions appear exactly when relevant without inflating every session's context.
lifecycle: Rule content is injected when Claude reads files matching the paths globs, not at launch and not on every tool use; rules without a paths field load at launch instead
failure_mode: The rule never fires when Claude creates a brand-new API file without first reading an existing matching file, so fresh endpoints can miss the conventions entirely
version_caveat: none for the core feature; edge cases have version floors (an invalid bracket pattern matches nothing instead of breaking Read only from v2.1.207; large brace expansions are budget-bounded from v2.1.217)

scenario: One engineer wants their personal habits (2-space indentation, conventional-commit messages, a preferred diff-review flow) applied in every repository they open on their machine, without pushing any of it onto teammates through shared repos.
primary: User-scope memory: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, optionally split into topic files under ~/.claude/rules/
rejected_alternative: A gitignored CLAUDE.local.md in each project
rejection_reason: CLAUDE.local.md is scoped to a single project, and because it is gitignored it exists only in the worktree where it was created. The user file at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md loads automatically for all projects on the machine and is never shared through the repo.
lifecycle: Loaded at session start in every project; user scope loads before project scope, so project instructions appear later in context and win on conflict
failure_mode: Project-level instructions can silently override the personal preference where they conflict, and the file spends context tokens in every session whether relevant or not

scenario: Claude keeps rediscovering the same repo quirks across sessions: which test target is flaky, that the dev server needs a Redis container, corrections the team repeats in chat. Nobody wants to maintain a document by hand; the knowledge should accumulate as a side effect of working.
primary: Auto memory (on by default): Claude writes a MEMORY.md index plus topic files under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/
rejected_alternative: Diligently curating the project CLAUDE.md after every session
rejection_reason: CLAUDE.md is written by humans and requires exactly the manual upkeep the team wants to avoid. Auto memory is the mechanism the docs define for Claude-written learnings from its own discoveries and your corrections, with the MEMORY.md index loaded automatically each session and detail moved to topic files read on demand.
context_boundary: main context (not loaded into subagents except conversation forks)
lifecycle: Claude saves and recalls notes during sessions; the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md load at every session start, topic files load on demand
failure_mode: Memory is machine-local and per-repository, so it never reaches teammates, other machines, or cloud sessions, and index content past the 200-line/25KB limit is dropped from startup loading

scenario: A support-ops group uses the CLI purely to draft incident communications, never to write code. They want every single response in a calm runbook voice with a fixed structure, and they want the built-in software-engineering behavior gone because it keeps steering answers toward code changes.
primary: A custom output style (a Markdown file in ~/.claude/output-styles or .claude/output-styles) with keep-coding-instructions left at its false default, selected via /config
rejected_alternative: An 'always respond in this voice and format' block in CLAUDE.md
rejection_reason: CLAUDE.md is delivered as a user message after the system prompt and cannot remove Claude Code's built-in software-engineering instructions. Output styles modify the system prompt itself, set role, tone, and default format for every response, and omit the coding instructions unless keep-coding-instructions: true. The docs explicitly route project knowledge to CLAUDE.md and voice/role changes to output styles.
context_boundary: main context (styles do not apply to subagents; only a fork of the conversation inherits the style)
lifecycle: Chosen via /config and saved as the outputStyle setting in .claude/settings.local.json; read once at session start, so a change takes effect after /clear or a new session
failure_mode: The style silently does not apply inside subagents, and on a style meant for coding work, forgetting keep-coding-instructions: true strips the built-in scoping and verification behavior
version_caveat: The standalone /output-style command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91; use /config or edit the outputStyle setting directly

scenario: Policy: no session may ever push to the protected main branch, full stop. A strongly worded instruction file has already failed twice, once right after context compaction. The guarantee must hold regardless of what the model decides.
primary: A PreToolUse hook with a Bash matcher that inspects the command and denies it (JSON permissionDecision "deny", or exit code 2 with the reason on stderr)
rejected_alternative: An unconditional rules file in .claude/rules/ stating the prohibition
rejection_reason: The memory docs state that CLAUDE.md and rules are context, not enforced configuration, and that blocking an action regardless of what Claude decides requires a PreToolUse hook. Hooks run deterministically at the tool-call boundary, outside model discretion, while rules can be ignored, deprioritized, or lost to context pressure.
lifecycle: Fires before every matching tool call, evaluated on each Bash invocation for the life of the session
failure_mode: A buggy hook fails open: exit code 1 is a non-blocking error, so only exit code 2 or an explicit deny decision blocks; matcher gaps (git invoked through a route the matcher misses) also leak

scenario: There is a long explainer of how the legacy billing engine works: its states, invariants, and the traps that bite people. Claude should pull it in whenever billing comes up in conversation, but it is pure background reference, not an action anyone should see or trigger from the command menu, and it is far too long to keep resident every session.
primary: A skill with user-invocable: false, its description tuned to billing-related requests so Claude loads it on topical relevance
rejected_alternative: A path-scoped rules file targeting the billing directories
rejection_reason: Path-scoped rules trigger only when Claude reads files matching the globs, but billing questions often start as conversation before any file is opened, and a triggered rule injects its whole body. A skill keeps only its description resident and loads the body when Claude judges it relevant; the docs name user-invocable: false for exactly this case, background knowledge like a legacy-system-context skill that is not a meaningful command for users.
lifecycle: Description always present in the skill listing; the full body loads when Claude invokes it; hidden from the user's slash-command menu
failure_mode: Discovery rides entirely on description matching: a weak description, or one truncated by the listing budget and the 1,536-character description cap, means the knowledge is never loaded

scenario: The security organization wants identical data-handling reminders and coding-style guidance present in every session on every developer machine, across every repository, and individual developers must not be able to opt out of it loading.
primary: Managed policy CLAUDE.md at the OS managed location (macOS /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md, Linux /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md, Windows C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.md), or the claudeMd key in managed-settings.json, deployed via MDM or config management
rejected_alternative: Pushing a ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md to every machine via dotfiles
rejection_reason: User-scope files belong to the user, who can edit or delete them, and ordinary CLAUDE.md files can be skipped with claudeMdExcludes. The managed policy file loads before user and project scopes in every session on the machine and is the one memory file the docs say cannot be excluded by individual settings.
lifecycle: Loaded at the start of every session on the machine, in every repository, before user and project instructions
failure_mode: It is still behavioral guidance, not technical enforcement: the docs' own split says anything that must be hard-blocked (tools, commands, paths) belongs in managed settings permissions.deny, not in the managed CLAUDE.md

scenario: Engineers keep pasting stack traces and issue details from our SaaS error-tracking service into the conversation by hand. We want Claude to query that service's live data directly, with each engineer signing in through the vendor's browser-based login instead of sharing a long-lived API key.
primary: Remote HTTP MCP server (claude mcp add --transport http) with OAuth 2.0 sign-in completed via /mcp or claude mcp login
rejected_alternative: A helper shell script or bundled executable that calls the vendor's REST API with a stored personal API key through the Bash tool
rejection_reason: The docs designate MCP as the integration path for external tools and data sources, with built-in OAuth 2.0: Claude Code runs the browser flow, stores tokens securely, refreshes them automatically, retries once after a refresh, and flags the server in /mcp when re-authentication is needed. A curl wrapper requires plaintext credential handling and provides none of that, and it exposes no typed tools, resources, or prompts.
lifecycle: server connects at session start; the model invokes its tools on demand (discovered via tool search by default); OAuth flow runs when the user authenticates via /mcp or claude mcp login
failure_mode: large tool outputs eat context (25,000-token default cap, warning at 10,000), and in non-interactive runs an unauthenticated server's tools stay unavailable until someone completes the OAuth flow in an interactive session

scenario: Claude keeps introducing type errors on our TypeScript codebase that it only discovers when the test suite finally runs. We want it to see compiler diagnostics immediately after each edit and to jump to definitions and references instead of grepping for symbol names.
primary: Install the official typescript-lsp plugin from the claude-plugins-official marketplace, with the typescript-language-server binary installed separately on each machine
rejected_alternative: Author a custom plugin containing an .lsp.json entry that launches typescript-language-server
rejection_reason: The docs explicitly direct users to install the pre-built LSP plugins for common languages (TypeScript, Python, Rust) from the official marketplace and to create custom LSP plugins only for languages not already covered. A hand-rolled config duplicates a maintained plugin, and if both end up enabled, only the first server registered for the .ts extension starts while the other is silently ignored with a /plugin warning.
lifecycle: language server starts when the plugin is enabled; diagnostics are pushed into Claude's context after each edit; navigation (go to definition, find references, hover) is available on demand
failure_mode: the plugin does not bundle the language server binary: without typescript-language-server on PATH the server fails with Executable not found in $PATH in the /plugin Errors tab and no diagnostics ever appear

scenario: Our platform team maintains a set of code-review helpers, reusable workflow commands, edit-time automations, and a shared external-tool configuration. Every engineer who clones any of our repositories should be offered the same set automatically and should receive updates whenever we publish changes.
primary: Package everything as a plugin, distribute it through a plugin marketplace (marketplace.json in a git repo), and reference it from each repository's .claude/settings.json via extraKnownMarketplaces plus enabledPlugins so teammates are prompted on workspace trust
rejected_alternative: Commit the raw .claude/ directories (commands/, agents/, skills/, hooks in settings.json) into every repository
rejection_reason: Standalone .claude/ configuration is documented as per-project, unversioned, and manually copied to share. The docs designate plugins plus marketplaces for exactly this need: sharing with teammates, versioned releases, reuse across projects, and automatic update tracking, with extraKnownMarketplaces prompting collaborators to install when they trust the project folder.
lifecycle: marketplace registration is offered when a teammate trusts the repo folder; plugins install and enable per enabledPlugins; updates flow via /plugin marketplace update and the plugin's version resolution
failure_mode: a version string pinned in plugin.json that nobody bumps means pushed changes never reach installers, and teammates who never accept the workspace trust dialog are never prompted, silently missing the tooling

scenario: We ship an internal deployment CLI, a compiled binary with many subcommands. Whenever our shared toolkit is active, Claude should be able to run it as a bare command inside ordinary shell pipelines, composing it with grep and jq across every project, without anyone editing their PATH.
primary: Ship the binary in the plugin's bin/ directory, which is added to the Bash tool's PATH while the plugin is enabled
rejected_alternative: Wrap the CLI in a stdio MCP server that exposes each subcommand as a separate MCP tool
rejection_reason: MCP tools have fixed input schemas and their results flow through MCP output limits, so they cannot participate in shell pipelines or compose with other commands. The plugin bin/ directory exists precisely for this: files there are invokable as bare commands in any Bash tool call while the plugin is enabled, keeping normal CLI ergonomics.
lifecycle: executables are on the Bash tool's PATH whenever the plugin is enabled; invocation happens through ordinary Bash tool calls under the normal permission flow
failure_mode: no structured schema constrains usage, so the model can misuse flags a typed tool would have prevented, and the command vanishes from PATH the moment the plugin is disabled, breaking workflows that assumed it

scenario: The tooling bundle we distribute internally changes daily. Teammates should automatically receive every merged commit as an update, with zero release bookkeeping on our side.
primary: Omit the version field from both plugin.json and the marketplace entry so Claude Code falls back to the git commit SHA as the version, treating every commit as a new version
rejected_alternative: Maintain a semantic version field in plugin.json and bump it for each release
rejection_reason: The version string is the cache key that decides whether an update exists: with an explicit version set, pushing new commits without bumping it has no effect and /plugin update reports already at the latest version. The docs' version-management table recommends commit-SHA versioning for internal or team plugins under active development and warn against explicit versions when iterating quickly.
lifecycle: version is resolved when /plugin update or auto-update fires: plugin.json version first, then marketplace entry version, then the git commit SHA, then unknown
failure_mode: every commit becomes an update, so teammates churn through half-finished work; and if someone later adds a version field for one release and forgets it, users freeze on that string while commits keep landing

scenario: We need Claude connected to an internal HTTP tool service that authenticates with short-lived tokens minted by our single-sign-on helper command. Tokens expire mid-session, and the service exposes no OAuth endpoints of its own.
primary: MCP server configured with headersHelper: a command that writes a JSON object of headers to stdout, run fresh at each connection and automatically re-run with one retry when a call returns 401 or 403
rejected_alternative: A static Authorization header in the server's .mcp.json entry using ${TOKEN} environment-variable expansion
rejection_reason: Environment expansion resolves once from the ambient environment, so an expired short-lived token leaves the connection failing until restart. The docs name headersHelper as the mechanism for authentication schemes other than OAuth, such as Kerberos, short-lived tokens, or an internal SSO, and Claude Code re-runs the helper, reconnects, and retries the call once on 401/403.
lifecycle: helper runs in a shell with a 10-second timeout at session start, on every reconnect, and on a 401/403 retry; there is no caching, so the script owns any token reuse
failure_mode: the helper executes arbitrary shell commands, so at project or local scope it only runs after the workspace trust dialog is accepted; a helper that exceeds 10 seconds or prints non-JSON breaks the connection entirely
version_caveat: automatic helper re-run and single retry on 401/403 requires Claude Code v2.1.193 or later

scenario: Whenever our shared toolkit is active in a session, Claude should hear about new lines appended to the application's error log as they appear, for the whole session, without anyone asking it to start watching.
primary: A plugin background monitor: an entry in monitors/monitors.json running tail -F, whose stdout lines Claude Code delivers to Claude as notifications for the lifetime of the session
rejected_alternative: A SessionStart hook whose command launches tail -F as a detached background process
rejection_reason: A hook command runs to completion per event and has no channel for delivering output that arrives later into the conversation, so the detached tail's lines never reach Claude. Monitors are the documented component that Claude Code starts automatically when the plugin is active, keeps running all session, and whose every stdout line is delivered to Claude as a notification, with the name field preventing duplicate processes on reload.
lifecycle: starts at session start and on plugin reload with when set to always, or on first dispatch of a named skill with on-skill-invoke:<skill-name>; runs for the session lifetime
failure_mode: monitors run only in interactive CLI sessions, run unsandboxed at hook trust level, do not load for project-scope skills-directory plugins, and keep running after the plugin is disabled mid-session until the session ends
version_caveat: experimental component: declared under experimental.monitors in plugin.json, and the schema may change between releases while it stabilizes

scenario: Security approved a third-party hosted integration for read-only use, but the vendor's sign-in service advertises write and admin permissions as well. We must guarantee that the credential stored on engineers' machines can never authorize a write, not merely that the assistant declines to perform one.
primary: Pin oauth.scopes in the server's .mcp.json entry (a space-separated string per RFC 6749) so Claude Code requests only the approved scope subset during the authorization flow and the issued token carries nothing more
rejected_alternative: Permission deny rules or a PreToolUse hook blocking the integration's write tools by name
rejection_reason: Deny rules and hooks constrain which tools the client calls, but the token in storage would still carry write scopes if granted, so any leak or bypass is a write credential. The docs call oauth.scopes the supported way to restrict an MCP server to a security-team-approved subset when the upstream authorization server advertises more scopes than you want to grant; the authorization server then issues a token limited to those scopes, with offline_access appended when advertised so refresh keeps working.
lifecycle: applies during the OAuth authorization flow; takes precedence over authServerMetadataUrl and discovered metadata; re-authentication after a 403 insufficient_scope reuses the same pinned set
failure_mode: a tool that legitimately needs a scope outside the pinned set fails with 403 insufficient_scope until you widen oauth.scopes and re-authenticate, and the pin silently overrides scopes supplied by a configured metadata URL
version_caveat: none for the pin itself; the related default of not requesting the full scopes_supported catalog changed in v2.1.196

scenario: Everyone working in one repository needs the same connection to our staging-database tool service, picked up automatically from a fresh clone, with each person consenting once before it first runs. No other repository will ever use this connection.
primary: A project-scoped MCP server: a .mcp.json file at the repository root, committed to version control, with Claude Code's built-in per-user approval prompt (resettable via claude mcp reset-project-choices)
rejected_alternative: Package the server configuration as a plugin and stand up an internal marketplace to distribute it
rejection_reason: For a single project the docs designate the checked-in .mcp.json project scope as the team-sharing path, complete with a per-user security approval flow before first use. A plugin plus marketplace adds hosting, install and enablement steps, and version machinery whose documented payoffs, reuse across multiple projects and versioned releases, this need explicitly lacks.
lifecycle: loaded from .mcp.json at the project root; each user approves it before first use; sits below local scope and above user scope in the name-matching precedence order
failure_mode: the server sits at Pending approval for each user until they approve interactively, and the config lives in exactly one repo: the day a second repository needs the same server, the entry gets copy-pasted and drifts, which is the point where a plugin becomes the right call
version_caveat: as of v2.1.196, enableAllProjectMcpServers or enabledMcpjsonServers committed in project settings cannot self-approve servers in a workspace the user has not trusted

scenario: Our distributed toolkit needs npm dependencies installed on each user's machine at first run, and those installed modules must keep working after the toolkit updates instead of being stranded or wiped when a new version lands.
primary: Install into ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}, the persistent per-plugin data directory under ~/.claude/plugins/data/, via a SessionStart hook that diffs the bundled package.json against a stored copy and reinstalls when they differ
rejected_alternative: Run npm install into ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} on first run and point the bundled server at that node_modules
rejection_reason: The plugin root is the versioned cache directory: its path changes on every update and the previous version's directory is removed about two weeks later, so the docs say to treat it as ephemeral and not write state there. ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} is documented for exactly this: installed dependencies such as node_modules or Python virtual environments that survive plugin updates and are deleted only on uninstall from the last scope (unless --keep-data).
lifecycle: the data directory is created on first reference, survives every plugin update, and is deleted when the plugin is uninstalled from its last scope; the install hook fires at SessionStart
failure_mode: because the directory outlives versions, a bare existence check misses updates that change the dependency manifest; skipping the documented manifest-diff pattern leaves users running new plugin code against stale dependencies

scenario: Our integration suite prints thousands of lines of logs. I want the suite executed and only the failing tests with their error messages to end up in my working conversation; the raw output is useless to me afterward and I will never reference it again.
primary: Delegate the run to a subagent (general-purpose or a custom test-runner agent): it does the noisy work in its own context window and returns only the summary to the main conversation.
rejected_alternative: Run the suite in the main conversation and rely on /compact afterward to reclaim the context.
rejection_reason: The verbose output still floods the main context first, and compaction is a lossy summarization pass rather than isolation. The sub-agents doc states the canonical use: when a side task would flood your main conversation with results you won't reference again, the subagent does that work in its own context and returns only the summary.
lifecycle: Agent tool delegation: Claude matches the task against subagent descriptions, or you ask for it explicitly or @-mention the agent
failure_mode: The returned summary omits a detail you need later, forcing a resume or re-run; and many subagents each returning detailed results can still consume significant main context.

scenario: I want a code-review worker for this repo that is structurally incapable of modifying the repository, no matter what its instructions say or what the model decides mid-task. It should only be able to read and search files.
primary: Custom subagent with a positive tools allowlist such as 'tools: Read, Grep, Glob' that omits Write, Edit, and Bash; the harness removes everything else from its tool pool.
rejected_alternative: Custom subagent with 'disallowedTools: Write, Edit' to deny the file-modification tools.
rejection_reason: The denylist inherits the rest of the pool: the docs' own no-writes example notes the subagent keeps Bash, MCP tools, and everything else, so it can still modify files through shell redirection or MCP tools. Only an explicit allowlist that excludes shell access gives the structural read-only guarantee (the built-in Explore agent works this way).
lifecycle: Tool filters are resolved when the subagent is spawned via the Agent tool or an @-mention; disallowedTools is applied first, then tools resolves against the remaining pool
failure_mode: An allowlist that still includes Bash (for example to run git diff) reopens a write path via the shell; misspelled entries can make the agent fail to launch; background runs silently narrow the built-in tool set further.

scenario: Mid-session I have a quick conceptual question about code we already walked through together. The answer should draw on everything discussed so far, needs no new file reads or commands, and neither the question nor the answer should take up room in the ongoing conversation history.
primary: /btw side question: it sees the full conversation context, has no tool access, and the answer is discarded rather than added to history.
rejected_alternative: Spawn a subagent to answer the question.
rejection_reason: A subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context and does not see the conversation history, so it lacks exactly the shared context the question depends on, and its result returns into the main conversation history. The sub-agents doc explicitly recommends /btw over a subagent for a quick question about something already in your conversation.
context_boundary: main context (full visibility, no tools, answer discarded from history)
lifecycle: explicit invocation with /btw followed by the question
failure_mode: No tool access means any question that actually needs a fresh file read or command cannot be answered; and because the exchange is discarded, you cannot build on the answer in later turns without restating it.

scenario: Two hours into a debugging session, I want to hand off drafting regression tests for the bug we just characterized. The helper needs all the accumulated findings, ruled-out hypotheses, config quirks, and stack traces from our discussion, and I do not want to re-explain any of it while I keep working on the fix.
primary: Conversation fork (/subtask, or the fork subagent type): it inherits the entire conversation history, system prompt, tools, and model, runs the side task in the background, and only its final result returns; it also reuses the parent's prompt cache.
rejected_alternative: Delegate to a named test-writer subagent with a delegation prompt summarizing the session.
rejection_reason: A named subagent starts from fresh context; the delegation message would have to compress two hours of nuance and would lose ruled-out hypotheses and quirks. The docs say to use a fork exactly when a named subagent would need too much background to be useful, and the fork's tool calls still stay out of the main context.
lifecycle: explicit /subtask <task> from the user, or Claude requesting the fork subagent type when fork mode is enabled
failure_mode: The fork inherits everything including wrong assumptions and context poisoning, so it gives no fresh perspective; it runs in the background by default, cannot spawn further forks, and steering it requires opening its transcript in the panel.
version_caveat: /subtask requires v2.1.212 or later (the command was /fork on v2.1.161 through v2.1.211); letting Claude spawn forks itself is experimental, controlled by CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT and a staged rollout

scenario: We have a written multi-step research procedure for summarizing pull requests that the team triggers by name. Its many intermediate file reads and command outputs must never land in the invoking conversation, and the procedure should run with read-only capabilities.
primary: Skill with 'context: fork' and 'agent: Explore' in the frontmatter: the SKILL.md content becomes the prompt driving an isolated subagent, and the Explore agent type supplies read-only tools (Write and Edit denied).
rejected_alternative: A regular inline skill (default context) containing the same step-by-step instructions.
rejection_reason: An inline skill's content and every resulting tool output land in the invoking conversation's context and stay there for the session. 'context: fork' creates a new isolated context, runs the skill content as the task, and returns only the result; the agent field picks the execution environment, and Explore is read-only by construction.
lifecycle: invoked by /skill-name or automatically by Claude via description match; the forked subagent spawns at invocation and by default runs in the background
failure_mode: The fork has no access to conversation history, so a procedure that depends on what was just discussed returns useless output; a backgrounded fork also runs with the narrower background tool set, and its edits (if any) fall outside /rewind checkpoints.
version_caveat: 'background: false' (wait for the result in the invoking turn) requires v2.1.218 or later; before v2.1.218 forked skills always blocked the turn

scenario: When we delegate endpoint implementation to a specialized worker, it keeps ignoring our API-conventions guide even though the main session has that guidance loaded. Every run of the worker must start with the full conventions text already in front of it, guaranteed, not merely discoverable.
primary: The subagent's 'skills' frontmatter field, which injects the full content of the listed skills into the subagent's context at startup.
rejected_alternative: Listing 'Skill' in the subagent's tools field so the worker can load the conventions skill itself.
rejection_reason: The docs call this out directly: to preload skills, use the skills field rather than listing Skill in tools. Listing the Skill tool only lets the subagent invoke skills on demand, leaving discovery to its judgment, which is exactly the failure observed; a fresh subagent context also never sees skills the main conversation already invoked.
lifecycle: injection happens at subagent startup, before the delegated task begins
failure_mode: Preloaded content costs tokens on every spawn even when irrelevant to the specific task; a listed skill that is missing, disabled, or marked disable-model-invocation: true is skipped with only a debug-log warning.

scenario: A reporting worker needs shell access to run database CLI queries, but any statement that mutates data (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, schema changes) must be deterministically blocked before it executes, even if the worker attempts one anyway.
primary: Subagent with 'tools: Bash' plus a PreToolUse hook in its frontmatter whose validation script inspects tool_input.command and exits with code 2 to block write statements (the docs' db-reader pattern).
rejected_alternative: Restricting via the subagent's tools or disallowedTools fields alone.
rejection_reason: Tool fields are all-or-nothing per tool: they can grant or remove Bash entirely but cannot allow SELECT while blocking INSERT within the same tool. The docs present PreToolUse hooks as the mechanism for conditional rules when you need to allow some operations of a tool while blocking others, with exit code 2 blocking deterministically.
lifecycle: PreToolUse fires before each matching Bash call while that subagent is active; frontmatter hooks are cleaned up when it finishes
failure_mode: Pattern-based validation can miss obfuscated commands; on macOS and Linux a script that is not executable makes the hook fail instead of blocking anything (fails open); project-level frontmatter hooks require workspace trust on v2.1.218+ or they are skipped.

scenario: We ship a long-running autonomous cleanup routine that users launch by name. While it is running, it must be impossible for it to interrupt the user with clarifying questions, and that capability should come back automatically once the user sends their next message.
primary: Skill frontmatter 'disallowed-tools: AskUserQuestion': the tool is removed from Claude's available pool while the skill is active, and the restriction clears on the next user message.
rejected_alternative: Skill frontmatter 'allowed-tools' listing every tool the routine should use, expecting unlisted tools to be unavailable.
rejection_reason: allowed-tools is a permission pre-approval, not a restriction: the docs state it does not restrict which tools are available and every tool remains callable. Only disallowed-tools removes tools from the pool, and the docs name exactly this use case: autonomous skills that should never call AskUserQuestion.
lifecycle: restriction applies from the turn that invokes the skill and clears when the user sends their next message; re-invocation re-applies it
failure_mode: The restriction is turn-scoped, so a workflow spanning multiple user messages silently regains the tool unless the skill is re-invoked; the field also cannot remove EndConversation while any other tool remains.

scenario: Five investigators should chase competing root-cause theories for a flaky-connection bug in parallel, and they must be able to message each other directly to try to disprove each other's findings and converge through a shared work list, rather than each just reporting back to one coordinator.
primary: Agent teams: teammates are independent Claude Code sessions with their own context windows, direct inter-agent messaging via mailboxes, and a shared task list with claiming and dependencies.
rejected_alternative: Spawning five parallel subagents from the main conversation.
rejection_reason: Subagents only report results back to the calling agent and never talk to each other, so the adversarial cross-challenge and self-coordination the scenario requires is structurally impossible; the docs' comparison table says to use teams when workers need to share findings, challenge each other, and coordinate on their own.
lifecycle: team forms when the first teammate is spawned after the user requests or approves it; teammates live for the session and shut down via shutdown requests or session end
failure_mode: Token cost scales linearly per teammate; /resume does not restore in-process teammates; task status can lag and block dependents; two teammates editing the same file overwrite each other.
version_caveat: experimental and disabled by default; gated by CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in settings.json or the environment

scenario: Our project rules file says vendor/ must never be read or searched, and work done directly in the session respects that. But whenever codebase exploration gets delegated out during research, the delegated searches keep touching vendor/ anyway.
primary: Restate the rule in the delegation prompt each time exploration is handed off: the built-in Explore and Plan agents skip CLAUDE.md files (and parent git status) by design, and the docs prescribe restating rules that must reach them. Delegating to a custom subagent instead also works, since every custom subagent loads the full CLAUDE.md hierarchy.
rejected_alternative: Strengthening or moving the rule within the CLAUDE.md hierarchy so the exploration delegate finally picks it up.
rejection_reason: No CLAUDE.md placement reaches the built-in Explore or Plan agents: they skip the entire hierarchy to stay fast and cheap, and the docs state there is no frontmatter field or per-agent setting to change which agents skip it. The rule works everywhere else, which is exactly why the misconfiguration persists unnoticed.
lifecycle: must be included at each delegation; nothing persists it into Explore's startup context
failure_mode: Purely advisory: one delegation that forgets the restatement silently violates the rule; a hard guarantee needs a different mechanism entirely, such as a permissions deny rule, a PreToolUse hook, or denying Agent(Explore).
version_caveat: none for the CLAUDE.md skip itself; v2.1.198+ optionally removes the built-in Explore and Plan agents with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPLORE_PLAN_AGENTS=1

scenario: Company policy says the assistant must never modify files under secrets/ or run shell commands that touch them, even when a crafted prompt or its own reasoning argues otherwise. Compliance wants a guarantee, not a convention it usually follows.
primary: PreToolUse hook (type: command) matched on Edit|Write and Bash that inspects tool input and returns hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision: deny, configured in settings.json
rejected_alternative: A CLAUDE.md rule stating 'never touch files under secrets/'
rejection_reason: The memory docs are explicit that CLAUDE.md and auto memory are context, not enforced configuration: 'To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook instead.' Hooks are evaluated by the client before the tool call executes, so the deny happens regardless of what the model decided; a memory instruction depends entirely on model compliance.
lifecycle: Fires on the PreToolUse event before every matching tool call; deny reason is fed back to the model
failure_mode: With only a CLAUDE.md rule, long-context drift or a prompt injection eventually produces one edit to secrets/ and nothing in the pipeline stops it; adherence degrades further as CLAUDE.md grows

scenario: Our release runbook is about 400 lines of ordered steps plus two helper scripts. It is needed roughly once a week, and the team resents that every conversation pays a token cost for it even during unrelated work.
primary: An Agent Skill: a .claude/skills/release-runbook/SKILL.md with a description, the procedure in the body, and the scripts as supporting files
rejected_alternative: Putting the runbook in the project CLAUDE.md (or an @-import from it)
rejection_reason: CLAUDE.md and its imports load in full at the start of every session; the skills doc says to create a skill 'when a section of CLAUDE.md has grown into a procedure rather than a fact' because 'a skill's body loads only when it's used, so long reference material costs almost nothing until you need it.' Only the skill's description sits in context until invocation.
lifecycle: Description is always listed to the model; full body loads when the model matches it to the task or the user types /release-runbook
failure_mode: As CLAUDE.md, the 400 lines consume context in every session; the memory docs warn files over ~200 lines reduce adherence, so both the runbook and the rest of CLAUDE.md get followed less reliably

scenario: During coding sessions the assistant should look up and update tickets in our self-hosted tracker, which sits behind OAuth. Copy-pasting ticket text into the chat is exactly what we are trying to eliminate.
primary: An MCP server for the tracker, added via claude mcp add / .mcp.json, exposing query and update tools with OAuth handled by the MCP authentication flow
rejected_alternative: A skill whose SKILL.md instructs Claude to call the tracker's REST API with bundled curl scripts
rejection_reason: The MCP docs describe exactly this trigger: 'Connect a server when you find yourself copying data into chat from another tool, like an issue tracker.' MCP gives typed tools, a managed OAuth flow, and per-tool permissioning; a script-based skill leaves credential storage, token refresh, and response parsing as hand-rolled shell plumbing.
lifecycle: Server connects at session start per its configured scope; the model calls its tools during turns subject to permission rules
failure_mode: The curl-skill version breaks on token expiry, requires secrets exposed to the shell environment, and every invocation is an unvetted Bash call rather than a scoped, individually permissionable tool

scenario: Every session opened in this repo should begin already knowing the current sprint's ticket list and the active git branch, pulled live at that moment from our tooling, without anyone asking for it or pasting it in.
primary: A SessionStart hook (type: command) that runs the queries and returns the results via hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext so they are injected into the session's context
rejected_alternative: Adding the sprint and branch information to the project CLAUDE.md
rejection_reason: CLAUDE.md is static text loaded from disk; it cannot execute commands, so the sprint list and branch would be stale the moment they change and would need manual editing. The hooks reference lists SessionStart's purpose as loading development context, with a git-branch injection as its worked example.
lifecycle: Fires on the SessionStart event (startup, resume, clear, compact); command output is injected before the first user turn is processed
failure_mode: The CLAUDE.md version silently serves last sprint's tickets and the wrong branch until a human remembers to hand-edit the file, which is worse than no context because the model trusts it

scenario: The platform team maintains a code-review helper, several lifecycle automations, and a tracker integration that about 40 repos across the org should all receive, with the ability to ship versioned updates that reach every consumer.
primary: A plugin (skills, agents, hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json in one directory with a .claude-plugin/plugin.json manifest) distributed through a plugin marketplace, private for internal use
rejected_alternative: Committing copies of the .claude/ directory (skills, agents, hooks in settings.json) into each of the 40 repositories
rejection_reason: The plugins doc draws this exact line: standalone .claude/ is for single-project and personal customization, plugins are for 'sharing with teammates, distributing to community, versioned releases, reusable across projects.' The manifest's version field plus marketplace installation gives controlled updates; namespacing prevents collisions.
lifecycle: Installed once from the marketplace per user or declared at repo level; components load whenever the plugin is enabled; bumping the manifest version propagates updates
failure_mode: The copy-paste approach drifts immediately: fixes must be re-copied into 40 repos, each copy mutates independently, and hook configs embedded in per-repo settings.json fall out of sync with the scripts they call

scenario: We scripted our production deploy as a repeatable procedure the assistant can execute, but it must only ever start when a human explicitly types the trigger. It must never begin because the assistant judged the code ready.
primary: A skill with disable-model-invocation: true in its frontmatter, invoked only as /deploy by the user
rejected_alternative: A regular skill with a description like 'deploys the application when the work is complete', relying on description matching plus a CLAUDE.md caution
rejection_reason: The skills doc names this case verbatim: use disable-model-invocation: true 'for workflows with side effects... like /commit, /deploy... You don't want Claude deciding to deploy because your code looks ready.' The flag removes the skill from the model's listing and blocks Skill-tool invocation, so only the human command path remains; a description-matched skill leaves the decision with the model.
lifecycle: Loads only when the user explicitly types /deploy; never surfaced to the model for automatic invocation
failure_mode: With a normal description-matched skill, a session where the user says 'looks done, wrap up' can match the description and trigger a real production deploy with no human decision in the loop

scenario: Whenever a new issue is opened in our GitHub repository, we want it triaged automatically: labeled, checked against likely duplicates, and given a first-response comment, with no human at a terminal anywhere in the loop.
primary: The Claude Code GitHub Action (anthropics/claude-code-action@v1) in a workflow triggered on issues: [opened], with the triage instructions in the prompt input (automation mode)
rejected_alternative: A hook, on the theory that hooks are the event-driven automation mechanism
rejection_reason: Hooks fire on Claude Code lifecycle events inside a running session (PreToolUse, SessionStart, Stop, and so on); no session exists when a GitHub issue is opened, so there is no event to hook. The GitHub Action is the documented mechanism for repo-event automation: it works with any GitHub event trigger and runs immediately when a prompt is supplied.
lifecycle: GitHub webhook (issues: opened) starts a workflow run; each run is a fresh non-interactive Claude Code execution on a CI runner
failure_mode: The hook version simply never runs: nothing in the repo listens to GitHub webhooks, so issues sit untriaged while the config looks superficially plausible
version_caveat: Use action @v1: the beta inputs (mode:, direct_prompt:, custom_instructions:) were removed in v1.0; mode is auto-detected and CLI options move into claude_args

scenario: A production bug has five plausible root causes. We want five investigators working simultaneously, each defending one hypothesis and actively trying to disprove the others' findings through direct back-and-forth, converging on a written consensus.
primary: An agent team: enable CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1, then have the lead spawn five teammates who share the task list and message each other directly over the mailbox system
rejected_alternative: Spawning five parallel subagents from the main session, one per hypothesis
rejection_reason: The agent-teams doc's comparison table is decisive: subagents 'report results back to the main agent only' and 'never talk to each other,' while teammates 'message each other directly' and self-coordinate on a shared task list. The requirement is peer-to-peer challenge, which subagents structurally cannot do; the docs even use competing-hypotheses debugging as the canonical team example.
lifecycle: Gated behind the CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 env var or settings entry; team forms when the lead spawns the first teammate with user approval; cleanup on session end
failure_mode: With subagents, each investigator reports one plausible theory to the orchestrator and no cross-examination ever happens; anchoring survives and the synthesized answer is just the first convincing hypothesis
version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default; requires CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1. Behavior described as of v2.1.178 (TeamCreate/TeamDelete removed); known limitations include no /resume of in-process teammates and one team per session

scenario: For a data-annotation project we want the assistant to act as a data analyst rather than a software engineer: every reply in a fixed tabular report format, with the default engineering behavior removed, applying to every turn of every interactive session in this project.
primary: A custom output style (.claude/output-styles/analyst.md without keep-coding-instructions), selected via /config or the outputStyle setting
rejected_alternative: Writing the persona and format rules into the project CLAUDE.md
rejection_reason: Output styles modify the system prompt itself and, by default, omit Claude Code's built-in software engineering instructions; CLAUDE.md is delivered as a user message after the system prompt and cannot remove those built-ins. The docs' comparison table assigns 'a different role, tone, or default response format every turn' to output styles and reserves CLAUDE.md for project conventions and codebase context.
lifecycle: Set once in settings (outputStyle) or via /config; read at session start, so changes take effect after /clear or a new session; applies to the main conversation only, not subagents
failure_mode: The CLAUDE.md version fights the still-present engineering system prompt: the assistant repeatedly drifts back to code-centric behavior and free-form answers, and the team keeps re-prompting for the report format
version_caveat: The standalone /output-style command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91; select styles through /config or the outputStyle setting instead

scenario: A CI job pipes each pull request diff to the assistant for a typo and lint pass. The output must be byte-for-byte reproducible no matter whose machine or which runner executes it; a teammate's personal automation or the project's tool-server config must not leak into the run.
primary: Headless invocation with bare mode: claude --bare -p with the prompt, --allowedTools for the needed tools, and any required context passed explicitly via flags
rejected_alternative: Plain claude -p in the CI script, reasoning that non-interactive mode is already isolated
rejection_reason: The headless docs state that without --bare, claude -p 'loads the same context an interactive session would,' including hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md from the working directory and ~/.claude. Bare mode exists precisely for 'CI and scripts where you need the same result on every machine': a hook in a teammate's ~/.claude or a server in the project's .mcp.json never runs because bare mode never reads them.
lifecycle: Explicitly invoked per CI run as a one-shot non-interactive command; only flags passed on that invocation take effect
failure_mode: Plain -p produces environment-dependent results: a developer's PostToolUse formatter hook or a project MCP server silently alters output on some machines, and the lint gate becomes flaky in a way that is nearly impossible to reproduce
version_caveat: --bare is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls and is slated to become the default for -p in a future release; until then, omitting it changes behavior

scenario: Every time the agent modifies a TypeScript file, our formatter must run on that file. We wrote the instruction into the project guidance the agent reads at startup, but every few sessions it skips the step and unformatted code lands in a commit.
primary: PostToolUse hook with an Edit|Write matcher whose command runs the formatter on the edited file path
rejected_alternative: A CLAUDE.md instruction telling Claude to always run the formatter after editing
rejection_reason: The memory docs state CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration, with no guarantee of strict compliance, and explicitly say that anything that must run at a specific point, such as after each file edit, should be written as a hook, which executes at fixed lifecycle events regardless of what Claude decides.
lifecycle: PostToolUse event fires after each successful tool call whose tool name matches Edit|Write
failure_mode: A matcher typo or a failing script skips formatting silently, because non-blocking hook errors do not stop the session; the hook also runs on every matching edit whether or not the file needed formatting.

scenario: Our repo contains .env files and a secrets/ directory holding live credentials. The agent must never be able to read those paths with its built-in tools, and the restriction should be checked into the repo so every teammate gets it automatically.
primary: permissions.deny rules such as Read(./.env), Read(./.env.*), and Read(./secrets/**) in the project's .claude/settings.json
rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook script that inspects file paths and blocks reads of the secret locations
rejection_reason: A custom hook reimplements what declarative deny rules already provide and misses coverage the rules get for free: Read deny rules also apply to @file mentions, Grep and Glob, IDE-shared context, and recognized Bash file commands like cat, head, tail, and sed. The settings docs' own secrets example uses permissions.deny, deny rules merge from every scope, and no allow rule or hook allow decision can override them.
lifecycle: evaluated by the permission system before every tool call; deny rules are checked before ask and allow, and deny/ask rules in project settings apply without workspace trust
failure_mode: Deny rules bind the built-in tools and recognized Bash file commands only; an arbitrary subprocess such as a Python script calling open() can still read the file, which only OS-level sandboxing prevents.
version_caveat: none for the core behavior; a Read deny rule additionally blocking the Edit tool on the same path requires v2.1.208 or later

scenario: Engineers kick off long agent runs and switch to other windows. They want an OS desktop alert the moment the run is blocked waiting for an approval or for input, without anyone watching the terminal.
primary: Notification hook, with matchers for notification types such as permission_prompt and idle_prompt, whose command fires the OS notifier
rejected_alternative: A Stop hook that sends the alert when Claude finishes responding
rejection_reason: Stop fires only when Claude ends its turn. A session blocked mid-turn on a permission prompt has not stopped, so a Stop-based alert never fires at the moment attention is actually needed. Notification is the documented event for permission prompts and idle waiting, and the hooks guide's first walkthrough is exactly this desktop-alert use case.
lifecycle: Notification event fires whenever Claude Code sends a notification; the matcher selects types like permission_prompt or idle_prompt
failure_mode: Notification hook output and exit code are ignored by design, so a broken notifier command fails completely silently: no alert and no surfaced error.

scenario: Security mandates that no developer may run the agent with approval prompting switched off entirely, and a developer must not be able to lift the restriction by editing anything in their own home directory or in any repo they control. The control has to hold on every laptop in the fleet.
primary: permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode set to "disable" in managed settings deployed to the OS-protected policy location (/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/ on macOS, /etc/claude-code/ on Linux, C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\ on Windows) via MDM or server-managed settings
rejected_alternative: Setting the same key in each developer's ~/.claude/settings.json or in the repo's .claude/settings.json
rejection_reason: The key works from any scope, but user, project, and local settings files are writable by the developer, who can simply delete the line. Managed settings are the only tier the precedence order says cannot be overridden by any other level, including command-line arguments, and the permissions docs state this key is typically placed in managed settings precisely because it can't be overridden there.
lifecycle: loaded from the managed policy source at startup (with live reload on change); governs which permission modes are selectable for the whole session
failure_mode: The guarantee is only as strong as the OS ACLs on the managed file location and the reach of the deployment tooling: a developer with local admin rights, or a laptop the MDM never touched, is outside the control.

scenario: Before the agent ends its turn and declares work complete, the test suite must have actually been run and passed during that turn; if not, the agent should be sent back to keep working. This must hold even when the model simply forgets to test.
primary: Stop hook that verifies tests ran and passed, and on failure exits 2 (or returns decision "block" with a reason) so Claude must continue working
rejected_alternative: A PostToolUse hook on Edit that reminds Claude to run the tests
rejection_reason: PostToolUse fires per tool call and cannot gate the end of the turn; it never fires at all when the model declares completion without making another tool call. Stop is the documented event for enforcing validation before accepting a response: its block decision prevents Claude from stopping and feeds the reason back so the conversation continues.
lifecycle: Stop event fires when Claude finishes responding; exit code 2 or decision "block" prevents the turn from ending and injects the reason
failure_mode: A hook that blocks unconditionally traps the agent in an infinite continue loop; the script needs a termination condition (such as checking the repeat-invocation flag in the hook input) or the session never ends.

scenario: We run the agent in a fully auto-approved configuration for speed, but any git push must still halt and wait for a human to explicitly confirm, every single time, no matter what approval configuration the session is running under.
primary: A permissions ask rule such as Bash(git push *), which forces a confirmation prompt on every matching call
rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision "ask" for git push commands
rejection_reason: bypassPermissions mode skips prompts except a documented exception list: explicit ask rules, connector tools an organization set to ask, and MCP tools marked requiresUserInteraction. Hook ask decisions are not on that list, so they carry no documented guarantee of surviving prompt-skipping modes, whereas content-scoped ask rules are additionally documented to force a prompt even for sandboxed commands in auto-allow mode.
lifecycle: evaluated before every matching Bash call in the fixed deny, then ask, then allow order; the prompt fires even in bypassPermissions and sandbox auto-allow
failure_mode: The gate requires a human present: in headless -p runs nobody can answer the prompt, and in dontAsk mode the call is denied outright instead of prompted, so unattended pipelines stall or fail at the gate.

scenario: Compliance needs an accurate record of every shell command the agent actually executed on developer machines, captured automatically with the full command line, rather than relying on the model to self-report what it ran.
primary: PostToolUse hook with a Bash matcher whose command appends the executed command and its result from the hook's stdin JSON to an audit log
rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook with a Bash matcher that logs each command
rejection_reason: PreToolUse fires before permission evaluation and before the call runs, so it records attempts that a deny rule, a hook, or the user subsequently blocked; the audit trail would contain commands that never executed. PostToolUse fires only after the tool call succeeds, and logging operations is one of its documented use cases.
lifecycle: PostToolUse event fires after each successful Bash tool call, receiving tool input and result on stdin
failure_mode: It captures successes only: commands that error need a companion PostToolUseFailure hook, and the log lives on each developer's machine unless the hook itself ships entries to central storage.

scenario: We want to shut off the entire aws CLI surface for the agent except one approved read-only invocation, aws s3 ls, which should go through without prompting. Every other aws command must be refused outright.
