primary: PreToolUse hook on Bash that inspects the command and returns permissionDecision "deny" for aws commands unless they match the approved invocation (returning "allow" for that one)
rejected_alternative: permissions.deny Bash(aws *) paired with permissions.allow Bash(aws s3 ls)
rejection_reason: Rules evaluate in fixed deny, then ask, then allow order and the first match wins; rule specificity does not change the order. The permissions docs state a broad deny like Bash(aws *) blocks every matching call including ones a narrower allow also matches, so a deny rule cannot carry allowlist exceptions. Exception logic must live in a PreToolUse hook, which the docs recommend for exactly this allow-everything-except pattern, and no deny rule for aws may remain in settings since deny rules override hook allow decisions.
lifecycle: PreToolUse event fires before each Bash tool call, ahead of permission rules and any prompt
failure_mode: The hook script must handle compound commands itself: a naive check passes 'aws s3 ls && aws iam delete-user', and the protection exists only on machines where the hook is configured.

scenario: Our path-based blocks stop the agent's own file tools from reading ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh, but a Python script it launches can still open those files directly. We need every process the agent spawns, including children of children, to be physically unable to read those paths.
primary: Enable the Bash sandbox (sandbox.enabled) with sandbox.credentials file entries or sandbox.filesystem.denyRead for the credential paths; Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux/WSL2 enforce the boundary on the process tree
rejected_alternative: Read deny rules such as Read(~/.aws/credentials) and Read(~/.ssh/**) in permissions settings
rejection_reason: The permissions docs warn that Read and Edit deny rules apply to Claude's built-in file tools and to file commands Claude Code recognizes in Bash, like cat, head, tail, and sed, but not to arbitrary subprocesses that open files themselves, and they point to enabling the sandbox for OS-level enforcement that blocks all processes from accessing a path.
lifecycle: OS-level boundary applied to every sandboxed Bash command and all child processes at execution time; subagents inherit the parent session's sandbox configuration
failure_mode: No native Windows support; the sandbox's default read policy still permits credential files until you explicitly deny them; and unless allowUnsandboxedCommands is set to false, the dangerouslyDisableSandbox escape hatch can rerun a failing command outside the boundary.
version_caveat: Sandbox runs on macOS, Linux, and WSL2 only (not native Windows); the sandbox.credentials block requires v2.1.187 or later

scenario: The platform team must guarantee that the only automation scripts, on-demand instruction packages, custom agent definitions, and external tool servers that ever load are the ones IT ships centrally. Nothing a developer adds on their own machine or commits into a repo may take effect.
primary: strictPluginOnlyCustomization in managed settings, which locks skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers to plugin or managed sources; paired with strictKnownMarketplaces and disableSideloadFlags to control the plugin channel itself
rejected_alternative: allowManagedHooksOnly in managed settings
rejection_reason: allowManagedHooksOnly blocks only user, project, and non-force-enabled plugin hooks; skills, custom agents, and MCP servers from user and project sources still load. strictPluginOnlyCustomization is the managed-only key documented to lock all four customization surfaces (or a named subset such as ["skills", "hooks"]) so they can come only from plugins or managed settings.
lifecycle: read from managed settings at startup; blocks loading of skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers from user and project sources for the whole session
failure_mode: Leaves bypass channels open unless companions are set: the --plugin-dir, --plugin-url, --agents, and --mcp-config CLI flags still work without disableSideloadFlags, and marketplace sources stay open without strictKnownMarketplaces; it also blocks developers' legitimate personal tooling, forcing everything through plugin packaging.
version_caveat: disableSideloadFlags requires v2.1.193 or later; no version gate is documented for strictPluginOnlyCustomization itself
